Thanks for the call today — great discussion. Quick recap + proposed next steps so we have a shared plan for integration and the RSP schema work: 

1) Recap from our side
- Use-case: customer support assistant that pulls context from the product DB, runs an embed+rbrk reranker, and then generates structured responses (JSON with action objects) that can trigger tools in the app.
- Traffic profile: bursty with medium QPS (~30 req/s peak). Latency SLO: 300ms p50 for 1-2k token sessions.

2) Action items (owners + ETA)
- Marissa: draft RSP request/response schema and example tool-calling pattern (attached) — by EOD 4/12.
- Acme: confirm auth flow (API key rotation / SSO) and routing preferences (region + fallbacks) — reply to thread.
- David (redwood infra): propose a canary rollout plan for embeddings+rerankers once schema is stable.

3) Specific technical questions we want answers to (see below for our suggested defaults)
- SDK setup and auth model (bearer token, rotation, short-lived creds)
- Routing: region header vs model pinning vs fallback behavior
- Structured output / tool calling: enforcing schema and validation
- Embeddings & reranking: when to call server-side vs client-side scoring
- Chat vs completions: when to use which endpoint for streaming semantics and token accounting
- Tokenization / max_tokens / stop semantics: best practices for predictable truncation

Hi Marissa / Alex,

Thanks for the recap. A few follow-up technical questions from our engineering team so we can validate the design:

1) SDK & auth
- Do you provide official SDKs for node/python/go or do we call a single REST endpoint? Any client-side token refresh helpers?
- For longer-lived clients (service accounts), what's the recommended approach for rotating keys and limiting blast radius (short-lived bearer tokens, mTLS, or KMS integration)?

2) Routing + model pinning
- We want all traffic from EU users to stay EU-first. Is that handled with an "X-Region" header, or do we pin callers to a model/region? How do fallbacks look if capacity in region is constrained?

3) Structured output/tool calling 
- We're planning to have the model return a JSON object with an array of "actions" (type, payload). How strongly do you recommend using Redwood's structured-output validator vs client-side schema validation?
- For tool-calls (e.g., call_ticket_api), do you recommend sending tool definitions in the prompt vs using a tool-calling API?

4) Embeddings & rerankers
- For our reranker: should we compute embeddings on-demand or cache them? Where do you do reranking (client vs server) for best latency/cost?
- What embedding dimensionalities do you recommend for semantic search at ~200k docs?

5) Request/response schema / chat vs completions / streaming
- If we use chat endpoints with streaming, how do you handle token accounting for "max_tokens" and stop sequences (we show partial tokens in the UI as they stream)?
- Any gotchas re. tokenization differences between chat/completions and the embedding tokenization step?
- Best practice for stop sequences with structured JSON output so we avoid truncated or malformed JSON?

Happy to hop on a short follow-up call — otherwise if you can reply on-thread with recommended defaults we can iterate.

Thanks,

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
To: Priya Shah <priya.shah@acme.com>, Alex Ford <alex.ford@acme.com>

Subject: Re: Acme integration: post-call architecture questions (chat vs completions, tokenization, streaming)

Thanks Priya — great questions. Below are our recommended defaults and notes based on production patterns we've seen. I'll also attach a short example payload for structured tool calling in the RSP draft.

1) SDK & auth (recommended)- We provide official SDKs for Node and Python (Go SDK in beta). SDKs wrap the REST API and include helpers for streaming, retries, and simple token rotation using short-lived creds.
- Auth model: prefer short-lived bearer tokens issued by your identity provider (OIDC) exchanged for Redwood service tokens. For server-to-server, you can use HMAC API keys with scoped permissions, rotated monthly, and backed by KMS for storage. For the highest security, use mTLS + KMS-managed keys.
- Rotation: our SDK supports a token-refresh hook; we recommend rotating service keys monthly and using short-lived tokens (1h) for public-facing clients.

2) Routing + model pinning
- Region routing is declarative: set X-Redwood-Region: eu or pin a region in the request body. If region capacity is constrained we provide automatic fallback to the next region in your policy (you can control fallback order). We log routing decisions in the Console so you can audit fallbacks.

3) Structured output / tool-calling
- Validator: use server-side validation in Redwood (we'll validate JSON against the schema and surface clear errors). This prevents malformed outputs from reaching your tooling. Client-side validation is good as a second line of defense but server-side is stronger.
- Tool calling: we recommend using the structured tool-calling API (send tool definitions in the call metadata). It avoids prompt bloat and is easier to enforce (Redwood will only allow outputs that match the tool schema). If you need human-provided tools at runtime, include a small tool manifest in metadata rather than full prompt text.

Example structured response (high-level):
{
  "response": {
    "text": "...generated answer...",
    "actions": [
      {"type": "create_ticket", "payload": {"summary": "..."}}
    ]
}

4) Embeddings & rerankers
- Cache embeddings for static docs. For user queries you compute embeddings on-demand. For 200k docs, use 1536-dim embeddings for a good precision/cost tradeoff; for higher precision at cost use 3072-dim. We recommend server-side reranking when you need to leverage fast ANN indexes (better latency at scale). Client-side scoring works for smaller collections or when you want full control.

5) Chat vs completions / tokenization / streaming
- Chat vs completions: use the chat endpoint when you have turn-based context or want to stream token-level responses. Completions is fine for single-shot prompts and simpler token accounting.
- Tokenization: tokenization is model-dependent (we publish tokenization rules per model in the catalog). Always reserve buffer space on "max_tokens" for your expected output + safety margin (we recommend adding 10-15% headroom). Example: if your prompt tokens = 600 and you need 800 token answer, set max_tokens >= 1200 to avoid truncation (allowing for model variability).
- Streaming and stop sequences: Streaming sends partial token deltas. Stop sequences are enforced server-side; when a stop token is emitted the stream closes. If you stream partial tokens to UI, implement a finalization step that requests the final response metadata (e.g., complete=true) or validate the returned JSON with the schema validator to detect truncation.
- For structured JSON, avoid using stop tokens that are ambiguous. Prefer schema validation + explicit "end_of_message" token in metadata. If you must rely on stop sequences, choose a unique delimiter that cannot appear in payloads (e.g., "<|end_of_response|>").

6) max_tokens and safety
- Use conservative max_tokens with a buffer; for streaming we also recommend a small finalization retry (non-streaming call) to fetch the complete output if validation fails. There is an extra cost for the retry but it prevents malformed tool calls.

7) Minor gotchas
- Embedding tokenization may differ slightly from generation tokenization; treat them separately when calculating costs.
- If you pin to a quantized model variant for cost, confirm that the structured-output validator is supported for that variant (most are).
